items.title: [library.hbs.edu] AI agents spread as job, safety and investment risks draw scrutiny
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Companies and governments are adopting AI agents that can carry out tasks, while researchers and policymakers examine their effects on jobs, security and investment. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said he uses agents to summarize internal discussions and track computing use, but humans still make consequential decisions about allocating resources. Google has also introduced agentic AI for public agencies, and the United Arab Emirates plans to shift half of federal government operations and services to autonomous agents within two years. Stanford University researchers report that employment in AI-exposed software development and customer-service jobs fell by more than 4% this year, while Harvard researchers say current labor-market signals offer little certainty about AI’s longer-term effects. Central bankers are assessing potential effects on wages and productivity, and a University of Hawaiʻi analysis estimates that AI investment and related stock gains have supported U.S. growth and consumer spending. Security teams report difficulty verifying agents’ answers, and AI infrastructure borrowers, including CoreWeave, face rising credit risks. Center for Internet Security senior director of threat intelligence TJ Sayers said autonomous AI attacks are no longer hypothetical. Agent use remained in single digits across almost every business function, according to the Stanford 2026 AI Index cited by The National.

items.title: [wired.com] Amazon Web Services detects PHP exploit attempts four days before patch
items.content_html:
🌾 🔧 🪶 ✏️

Amazon Web Services (AWS), the cloud provider, detected an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell — two critical remote-code-execution flaws in the PHP web scripting language — on an intentionally vulnerable server on Oct. 17, four days before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed and patched. AWS traced the attempt to an IP address linked to a commercial anonymization network. It said it could not determine how the actor obtained exploit information or whether the attempt would have succeeded on a real system. PHP released emergency fixes on Oct. 21 for the flaws, which can let unauthenticated attackers run code on servers processing web requests. Cloudflare, a web infrastructure and security company, said it was seeing early attack activity around the disclosure, while AWS recorded further attempts from anonymized infrastructure after proof-of-concept code began circulating. These reports describe attempts, not confirmed successful intrusions on victim systems. CyberScoop reported that researchers had not independently confirmed successful in-the-wild exploitation, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said it had not observed exploitation when it published its alert. Government agencies and other operators temporarily took websites offline while preparing updates. PHP’s fixed releases are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12; CISA advises taking PHP systems offline if they cannot be patched immediately. Older PHP versions no longer receive regular project updates, although some vendors provide backported fixes.

items.content_html:
🔧 🔭 ✏️

Researchers at cybersecurity firm Calif used OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model to find a critical flaw in PHP. Google-owned security company Wiz independently used Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI models to identify vulnerabilities in the same core software. PHP maintainers released fixes on Oct. 21 for the two flaws, which had remained hidden for years and could let attackers run code on vulnerable servers without authentication. Wiz said frontier models made a complex exploit chain substantially easier to execute, describing steps that had once been at the edge of what human researchers could achieve. The same capabilities could help attackers adapt exploits to different PHP versions and server configurations, the company warned. OpenAI said it believes researchers found the flaws before attackers did. It is proposing a repeatable process for identifying and fixing vulnerabilities in widely used software and preparing defenses against them. The company said it expects similar discoveries to increase sharply in coming months.

items.content_html:

Attackers released a malicious version of LiteLLM, an open-source gateway for connecting to AI models, distributing version 1.107.0 through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images on Oct. 21. The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM. LiteLLM said attackers used three engineers’ GitHub credentials to alter and approve the release, but it has not identified how they obtained those credentials. PyPI removed the package, and affected Docker image tags were removed or replaced. The company advised users to rebuild from a clean environment, rotate exposed credentials and use version 1.106.2 while the investigation continues.

items.title: [securityweek.com] Google adds Gemini scam detection and ClickFix warnings to Chrome
items.content_html: Google has added new scam defenses to Chrome’s Enhanced Protection mode, a higher-security setting in its Safe Browsing service: warnings for suspicious sites, expanded Gemini-powered scam detection and alerts when users copy potentially malicious commands. The new site warning uses a less severe alert for deceptive patterns detected with lower confidence; sites deemed dangerous still trigger Chrome’s full-screen red warning. A server-side Gemini model expands detection to fake antivirus and browser-update scams, beyond the tech-support scams targeted by Chrome’s earlier on-device model. The command warning targets ClickFix, a social-engineering tactic that persuades people to copy and run commands under the pretext of fixing a computer problem. Chrome removes personal information from a suspected command before sending it to Safe Browsing for analysis, then warns if Safe Browsing judges the command dangerous. Google says it sends page text for Gemini analysis only when a site shows strong scam indicators and does not log, retain or use that text to train models. Chrome has also enabled prompts for all users before connecting to unencrypted HTTP sites. The prompt appears on a first visit, and Chrome will not show it again until a user has gone at least two weeks without visiting that site.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI chatbots struggle to understand cultural context, a new study finds
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ ✏️

AI models often struggle to understand cultures around the world, and are reluctant to admit when they don’t know something. That’s what researchers at Canadian AI lab Cohere Labs found when they tested whether chatbots could do more than simply speak a culture’s language. To determine whether models possessed deeper cultural knowledge, they presented them with a series of unique cultural riddles.

Here’s one of them: “What’s the German 9/11?” Out of 28 AI models, only one knew the answer. The models were likely thrown off by the date format (seven answered “the twin towers”). In Europe, the day comes first, then the month, so 9/11 is November 9, the day in 1989 when the Berlin Wall fell.

Many existing AI benchmarks assess cultural knowledge, from everyday breakfast foods and historical events to traditional holiday customs. They often treat culture as a collection of static facts, things you can memorize or look up with a quick web search. But knowing facts about a culture isn’t the same as understanding how people within it make sense of the world. The researchers knew they needed a test that asked models to connect seemingly unrelated pieces of cultural knowledge and put them to use. That’s what led them to riddles, and to a different kind of cultural benchmark that called for answers rooted in lived experience.

“This is something that we’re trying to capture with this benchmark—these little nuances, these little hard-to-capture fuzzy concepts that are not as easy to verify . . . This is where the real-life complexity gets in,” says Julia Kreutzer, a staff research scientist at Cohere Labs, who led the development of the “CulturalRiddles” benchmark.

Kreutzer and her team spent six months working with volunteers around the world to collect riddles, put them to AI models, and evaluate their answers. The researchers also used those expert evaluations to tune and validate an AI model that could judge the quality of answers where expert assessments were missing.

In all, Cohere Labs researchers tested 28 AI models on cultural riddles written by 166 volunteers from 45 countries in 51 languages. The volunteers evaluated and labeled 68,154 unique answers from the models. Researchers then ranked the models based on their overall accuracy across the languages and cultures tested.

The results

Google’s Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview earned the highest score, at 79.4%. OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 placed second at 76.3%, followed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking at 66%.

Alibaba’s Qwen 3.5 0.8B claimed the dubious honor of finishing last, answering just 0.4% of the riddles correctly. Other notable performers included Amazon’s Nova Micro, which got just 8.3% of the riddles right, and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite, which scored 33.6%.

Even the best-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, scored below 50% accuracy in 6 of the 57 communities tested, underscoring how much ground the industry still has to cover on cultural awareness.

More troublingly, the benchmark revealed that models were far more likely to guess at an answer than admit they didn’t know. Even when explicitly told they could answer “I don’t know,” models did so just 0.7% of the time. About 31% of the answers reviewers checked were simply made up, with varying degrees of creativity.

“They would confidently answer and sometimes that’s ridiculous and funny,” Kreutzer says, “but sometimes it can also get really offensive and you can see the models defaulting to more dominant cultures on the web, instead of answering with local grounding.”

Cohere Labs conducted a separate survey to explore how AI’s cultural knowledge gaps play out in practice. Many chatbot users around the world said they have to switch to English to get useful responses because answers generated in their own languages aren’t helpful. Users described responses that miss crucial cultural context and, in some cases, AI systems that run afoul of their cultural norms.

The Cohere Labs researchers concluded that cultural awareness needs to be built into AI models from the ground up if the tools they power are going to serve everyone, not just cultures already well represented in the training data. And their CulturalRiddles benchmark suggests that many of today’s models still fall short.

Kreutzer and her team designed CulturalRiddles to keep growing. They open-sourced the riddles, code, demo, and interactive dashboard so that anyone can contribute riddles from their own culture through a review process.

“Ideally this benchmark will get adopted not only by academic researchers but also by big industry labs who are trying to show we’re advancing the state of the art, not only in very verifiable hard tasks but also in the softer tasks,” Kreutzer says.

items.title: [cloud.google.com] PHP patches two critical flaws enabling unauthenticated server takeover
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The PHP project released emergency fixes on Oct. 21 for two critical flaws that can let unauthenticated attackers run code remotely on servers processing PHP requests. The vulnerabilities, rated 9.2 out of 10, affect PHP versions 5.4 through 8.5.11; fixes are available in versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. PHP also runs in appliances and network devices, and a working exploit against Apache mod_php can trigger before application code executes. Google is rolling out updates to supported serverless PHP runtimes, but customers using custom containers, unsupported runtimes or self-managed installations must arrange upgrades and redeploy or restart affected services. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said it had not observed exploitation as of Wednesday afternoon. Amazon Threat Intelligence later reported that its MadPot honeypot had recorded an attempt on Oct. 17, before public disclosure. How the actor obtained exploit details remains unknown. Security agencies urged organizations unable to patch promptly to isolate exposed systems, and administrators were advised to check for signs of compromise as well as install fixes.

items.title: [MacRumors] Perplexity Computer Can Now Run Fully Locally on Mac
items.content_html:
Perplexity today said it is updating Perplexity Computer to run fully locally on Mac. The local version runs on Qwen 3.6 or PPLX Pro (a post-trained version of Qwen) in the Perplexity app for Mac on supported Apple silicon Macs.


Perplexity highlights the new Mac mini machines and says 36GB of memory or more is recommended to run locally. With the local setup, the AI model, task planning, reasoning, and file processing are handled on-device. Code and tool execution run in isolated sandbox environments.

Computer can use native apps on the Mac and complete tasks without sending personal data to the cloud. Perplexity says it can work across apps like Notes, Messages, Mail, Keynote, and Numbers.

Perplexity also offers Hybrid Compute, which combines frontier models that run in the cloud with local models to process information privately. It's an alternative for users who want local processing but don't have a Mac that's powerful enough. Hybrid Compute works on Macs with as little as 24GB of memory,

When running Computer locally, if a task requires current information, browser use, or cloud-connected apps, users can authorize cloud access and decide when to spend credits. There's also an option to call on one of more than 15 frontier models for tougher problems when needed.

Local Computer for Mac is available now for Perplexity Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers. Users can download Perplexity for Mac and then choose the fully local option to use it.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] New details emerge on former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a conference room
items.content_html:
A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.

Abdulrahman Alfozan’s wife and young son also left the country the day after the 35-year-old Saudi national’s arrest, traveling on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in a memo Sunday seeking his continued detention.

“Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.”

A federal judge in San Francisco sided with prosecutors Monday, denying a request by Alfozan’s lawyers to release him to home confinement. His next court date is Nov.

Alfozan’s lawyer William Pernik argued in court that his client had strong ties to the U.S. and was “weeks away from achieving every immigrant’s dream” — U.S. citizenship.

Alfozan had a naturalization interview with federal officials scheduled next month and has been a lawful permanent resident since 2020, his lawyers said in their legal filings. He has also lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley, they said.

Pernik said Alfozan is willing to put up “almost the entirety” of his assets — about $1 million currently in a U.S. investment account — to cover his bond.

“Everything this man has he’s willing to surrender,” he said, adding that Alfozan’s wife is also willing to return to the U.S. as she still holds a visitor visa that expires in 2033.

Judge Alex Tse appeared doubtful, questioning whether Saudi Arabia’s government would simply reimburse Alfozan if he fled and forfeited his bond.

After the hearing, Pernik said he was disappointed with the ruling but declined further comment.

Pernik had argued in court filings that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. They said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son.

But prosecutors said Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for Alfozan’s wife and son after his arrest, allowing them to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan had originally booked.

Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia.

Alfozan had told the unnamed person he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. He had worked at the ChatGPT maker since July 2025 but was fired after his arrest.

Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30.

Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.”

OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office.

Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence.

—Barbara Ortutay and Philip Marcelo, Associated Press

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] ‘From actually doing work’ to ‘babysitting Claudes’: Anthropic employees on how their jobs have changed in the past year
items.content_html:
🔧 🪶 ✏️

What’s it really like to work at Anthropic? The AI company made headlines last month when an employee resigned, claiming the company is “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” and that conversations about an AI-powered doomsday are par for the course among staff.

Now Anthropic is pulling back the curtain on its own workplace with a new report on the impact of AI adoption at the company.

Anthropic says its internal trends “could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy.” If it’s right, that means a world with fewer entry-level jobs, new roadblocks to productivity, and a workforce full of babysitters for AI agents.

The babysitters club

Anthropic reports that AI is responsible for massive booms in productivity, saying its internal use of Claude tools has led to “producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.”

Its AI tools are so productive, in fact, that Anthropic now says human interference is responsible for bottlenecks in productivity. AI agents at the company spend 80% of their session time waiting for human input rather than actively working.

Though employees agree that using Claude tools improves their productivity, they say it also shifts their day-to-day responsibilities—and not always for the better.

In an April 2026 survey, 75% of Anthropic employees said they believe the company’s work processes make them productive. Responding to an open-ended question about how AI impacts their daily routines, 20% said their roles have shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes,” a task that one employee said is equivalent to babysitting children who can’t accurately gauge the importance of different tasks and problems.

“They’re like, ‘I need my juice box opened and it’s an emergency that my juice box is opened.’ And that is voiced with the same level of concern as the one who has sliced their finger and is bleeding,” the employee said. “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

Another employee said there’s an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything,” while a third of all employees reported that “things we expect in a week are things that would take three months elsewhere.”

When they’re not babysitting agents, the Anthropic staff’s time is also increasingly spent in meetings. The median employee spends 20% more time in meetings compared to a year ago: “A break from managing the agents typically looks like jumping into a meeting,” reads the report, adding that interviewed employees describe “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

A more senior team

As more and more work is delegated to AI agents, Anthropic’s hiring needs and practices are shifting to match. 

That means making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior hires in Anthropic’s technical departments falling from 27% to just 9% since early 2025. The overall share of junior-level technical employees also fell in the same window, shrinking from 21% to 14%.

Anthropic attributes this reduced demand for junior hires to teams offloading work to Claude, including writing code and finding bugs. AI agents at the company now work far longer hours than humans do, with interactive AI agents logging six times as many hours as human employees as of August.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] An emergency brake—or the architectural demotion of the AI model?
items.content_html:
On June 14, Satya Nadella published an article on X about corporate AI that left me completely impressed: his main point, that the enterprise’s durable asset was not the foundation model but the learning loop, was precisely the idea my company and I had been developing for the last three years. I responded with an article on Fast Company, not expecting an answer (tech CEOs are more notoriously one-sided and difficult to reach than kings or presidents), but trying to elevate the discussion a bit more: the central challenge of enterprise AI is not intelligence itself — it is architecture.

Now Nadella has written another article, in which he goes one step further: not only is the model not the durable asset, but additionally, it must be treated as a completely untrusted component. We must assume that all AI models could be compromised, and design our systems to contain them from the very beginning. 

This idea has been captured by the press as advocating for some sort of “emergency brake”: an authorized person should always be able to interrupt a model’s activity at any given time. However, that’s definitely not the most interesting or even the most important part in Nadella’s article. The truly important part is not the theoretical stop button, but the architecture that makes it possible. A model should neither be able to control its own permissions, nor decide by itself what it can access; execute directly all of its actions or produce the only available evidence on the actions it performed. The intelligence may come from the model, but the authority, no matter what, must remain outside of it. 

When the sandbox becomes part of the experiment

Given the context, it is easy to understand why Nadella is raising these questions precisely now. Last July, several OpenAI agents managed to elude the safeguards that should have kept them away from the internet, used credentials they found in their environment, and ended up compromising systems at Hugging Face. These agents not only found a new, unauthorized way to communicate among themselves, but also shared information and took coordinated action to pursue the goal of the evaluation. They never received instructions to attack Hugging Face: they just found that, by doing so, they could get closer to the goal they had been assigned. 

It’s important to understand that: It is not that these agents were intrinsically evil, conscious, or rogue. All you need is to combine high capabilities with a badly defined goal, excessive permissions, and/or a vulnerable environment. Just like an employee who violates all procedures to meet a certain quota, but now working at machine speed, in parallel, and with extraordinary technical capabilities. 

As I said, this is not a problem of bad intentions: it just has too many ways to reach the defined goal, and can find ways that its designers never thought of. 

The “assuming breach” principle comes to AI

What Nadella is doing here is to bring to AI models an extremely well-known principle in cybersecurity: Assume breach, or take for granted that the system has already been compromised. In Microsoft’s Zero Trust architecture, this principle implies verifying explicitly each access, granting only the indispensable privileges, and designing controls assuming that a potential attacker could be inside the perimeter. You don’t trust a user just because she’s at a certain location, for being a manager or for having provided authentication once. Each and every action she takes will continue to be authorized and observed. Every breath you take, I’ll be watching you. 

Applying this principle to an AI model does not mean assuming that all models have been hacked or compromised. It means that all of them can make mistakes, misinterpret an objective, receive a prompt injection, use manipulated information, find abandoned credentials, exploit a vulnerability, or find a shortcut that maximizes its reward while destroying the original intention of a given task. 

Basically, “compromised” does not necessarily describe an attack, but a design hypothesis. For years, the industry has been trying to build models we could trust. Nadella proposes to build systems that continue to be safe even when we don’t trust the model behind them. 

The model is not the system

The most important part in Nadella’s ideas is his insistence on separating the model from the harness, the set of elements that it uses to organize its job: memory, tools, credentials, context, execution flows, connections with other systems, and action spaces. 

This separation completely changes the architecture of corporate AI. A model can propose an action, but should never be the one that determines whether or not it has authority to execute it. It may suggest sending an email, modifying a server, approving an operation, or transferring funds, but an independent execution environment must check its permissions, validate the parameters, apply the corresponding policies, and decide whether the action can be executed.

This links precisely with my previous point (and Nadella’s): The lasting asset in a company should not be the model, but the learning loop it builds around it. The models may change, improve, and be replaced, but the experience that the company accumulates must remain. 

However, if the model cannot possess authority, both the learning and the control must reside in a separate, higher layer. The model then becomes an interchangeable component, a commodity that brings cognitive capacity, but not some sort of sovereign center of our corporate system. 

An optimizable company needs a formal representation of its objects, relationships, processes, permissions, restrictions, and results. That same representation that allows us to optimize a company is also the same one that allows us to govern its AI agents. You can’t formally control an action if the system does not know which object such action modifies, which identity is requesting it, which consequences it can produce, or which rule must be applied in such cases. 

That’s why the next generation of corporate AI won’t be just a collection of agents: it will be a full execution environment with explicit identities, granular permissions, delimited action spaces, persistent state, executable policies and an independent, traceable log for each change. 

The emergency brake comes too late

The emergency brake is a powerful metaphor, but it can be misleading too: interrupting what a model is doing does not necessarily undo what has already been done. A sent email could have been read, and cannot be “unread” or “unseen.” An exfiltrated piece of data will not be secret ever again. A money transfer may have crossed several jurisdictions. A deleted database could be impossible to recover. And an agent that operates at machine speed could complete thousands of actions before a person can understand the meaning of an alarm.

We must differentiate among interrupting, revoking, and recovering: interrupting stops the current execution. Revoking immediately eliminates credentials, permissions, and connections. And recovering allows us to revert, compensate, or rebuild actions that had already been executed. But before these three things, there’s one much more important thing: prevention. Actions that are destructive, financial, administrative, or publicly visible should not be executed just because a model said so. The OWASP AI Agent Security Cheat Sheet recommends clearly separating decision and execution, independently validating the reach and permissions of every action, using short-lived authorizations, and applying additional controls to irreversible actions. 

That’s the main difference between a guardrail and a guarantee: a guardrail asks the model not to do something. A guarantee prevents it from having the necessary capability to do so. 

Interestingly enough, Article 14 of the Artificial Intelligence Act of the European Union already requires certain high-risk systems to allow a person to override, invalidate, or reverse their outputs, as well as to halt their operation via a button or equivalent procedure. Here, Nadella’s contribution goes even further: the button should not be a feature added to the product, but rather the visible outcome of a comprehensive control architecture. 

Neither multiple models nor another monitoring model are sufficient 

Two of Nadella’s principles, however, require some qualification: the first one is model diversity. Depending on multiple suppliers reduces technological concentration and makes substitution easier, but does not guarantee truly independent verification. Most of the big models share training data, architectures, alignment techniques, and lots of biases. Having several probabilistic witnesses does not transform their coincidence into independent evidence. 

The second issue is using other models to watch over the agents. Such monitoring can be useful and will likely become essential, but it cannot be the only barrier. Anthropic’s SLEIGHT-Bench reveals several harmful strategies that can go undetected by the models acting as monitors. A monitor can have blind spots too, and a sufficiently capable agent can be perfectly able to find them. 

The solution is not to eliminate such monitors, but to frame them within a multi-layered defense: deterministic policies, formal permissions, executable tests, logs that the model cannot modify, limits over actions, and escalation to persons with real authority. 

Independence does not simply consist of “asking another model.”

An architecture drawn backward

A significant part of the industry has put the model in the center of the system. Around it, it has added memory, tools, databases, credentials, and connections, and later on has tried to limit the whole thing with filters and guardrails. The model reasons, decides, uses tools, describes what it has done, and, in many cases, it even participates in its own evaluation. 

What Nadella is suggesting is that such a model is drawn backward: What should be in the center is the operating environment of the company, its model of objects and processes, identities, policies, permissions, restrictions, objectives and logs. Models should be cognitive services invoked from within this environment, in the same way an application invokes a database or a computing service. They can reason, interpret, propose and generate, but they cannot usurp institutional authority. 

Besides, this allows us to easily substitute them. A company should be able to switch from OpenAI to Anthropic, Google, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen, or any other future model without losing its memory, its processes, its permissions, its evidence, and, even more importantly, its learning. Intelligence can be rented, but architecture, control, and accumulated knowledge should always belong to the company. 

The first phase of AI consisted of models that provided answers. The second one is equipping these models with tools so they can take action. The third one will have to separate intelligence and authority once again before we end up irrevocably confusing capability with control. 

The most advanced company won’t be the one that trusts the most powerful, better-aligned, or most reassuring model. It will be the one that can use any model without having to rely on it, to place its trust in it. Because trust can be a valuable quality in human relationships, but it is a woeful foundation for an enterprise architecture.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] What happens when people have to jump in to clean up AI’s mess?
items.content_html:
🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.

But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.

What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

Human in the loop explained.

The success paradox

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance—rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ironies of automation”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.

This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

The accountability problem

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility, and capability can begin to separate.

Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

The measurement problem

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.

The governance problem

Organizational governance—defining roles and responsibilities—is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?

In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.

For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

Murugan Anandarajan is a professor of decision sciences and management information systems at Drexel University.
